books.title: Foundation Mathematics
books.subtitle: From counting to the doorstep of algebra
books.description: The ground floor of mathematics, built patiently from the act of counting: numbers and place value, the four operations and why they work, factors and primes, fractions, decimals and percents, ratio and proportion, elementary geometry and measurement, and the first taste of algebraic thinking. Every idea is introduced from zero, derived where a derivation exists, and drilled through graded exercises with full solutions — so that the books above it (Arithmetic & Number Systems, Elementary Algebra, Geometry…) can be climbed without gaps.

chapters.title: Numbers and Place Value
chapters.summary: Starts from the act of counting itself: what a number is, how numerals encode them with just ten digits, why place value makes the whole system powerful, and how the number line lets us see order at a glance. Closes with the two great naming conventions for large numbers — international and Indian.

lessons.title: Numbers, Digits and Place Value
lessons.unit: platform base (lesson 1.1 authored with the platform as pipeline validation)
concepts: International and Indian systems of numeration
objectives: Say precisely what a number, a numeral and a digit are — and never confuse them again
Break any whole number into its place values and write it in expanded form
Read and compare numbers in both the international and the Indian naming systems
Locate integers on the number line and use it to compare them

lessons.title: Comparing and Ordering Numbers
concepts: Digit count as the first comparison test
The domination bound: why the leftmost differing seat decides
Greatest and smallest numbers from given digits
Digit rearrangements preserve the digit sum
objectives: Compare any two whole numbers instantly and say which seat decided the answer
Arrange a mixed list of large numbers in ascending or descending order without pairwise struggle
Build the greatest and smallest possible numbers from a given set of digits
Explain, with a proof, why the leftmost differing digit always settles the comparison

lessons.title: Rounding and Estimating
concepts: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred and thousand
The midpoint convention: ties round up
When to round up on purpose (capacity problems)
objectives: Round any whole number to a named place and say which digit made the decision
Estimate sums, differences and products to a chosen level of coarseness — and choose the right level
Recognise when rounding a subtraction of close numbers destroys the answer, and what to do instead
State a guaranteed error bound for a sum of rounded numbers

chapters.title: The Four Operations
chapters.summary: Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — first as actions on quantities, then as algorithms on numerals, where the overflow argument from Chapter 1 returns as carrying and borrowing. Includes order of operations, estimation checks, and why division by zero is undefined.

lessons.title: Addition and the Art of Carrying
concepts: Why the carry is never more than 1
objectives: Explain addition as counting on, and show it as a jump on the number line
State and use the commutative, associative and identity properties of addition
Execute column addition with carries reliably — and prove why a carry can never exceed 1
Use the mod-9 digit-sum checksum to catch errors, and know exactly when it fails

lessons.title: Subtraction and Borrowing
concepts: Subtraction as the inverse of addition
Subtraction breaks closure, commutativity and associativity
Why one borrow is always enough
The inverse check and the nines complement
objectives: Explain subtraction as the missing-addend question — the inverse of addition — and read it as take-away or comparison
Show exactly which laws of addition die for subtraction, with a counterexample for each
Execute column subtraction with borrowing reliably, including the borrow-across-zeros ripple
Prove why a column ever needs to borrow exactly one — never two — and check any subtraction two independent ways

lessons.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition — and Beyond
concepts: Equal jumps on the number line
The laws that return: closure, commutative, associative, identity 1
Column multiplication as shifted partial products
objectives: Explain multiplication as repeated addition and as equal jumps on the number line — and why the two orders land in the same place
State the four laws multiplication shares with addition plus the new distributive law, and use each deliberately
Execute column multiplication as shifted partial products, knowing why the shift exists and how large its carries may grow
Bound a product's digit count before computing it, and check any product with the mod-9 fingerprint

lessons.title: Division, Remainders and Why Zero Never Divides
concepts: Sharing and grouping — the two readings
Equal jumps backwards: division as repeated subtraction
Division as the inverse of multiplication
The division algorithm a = q·b + r
Why division by zero is undefined
objectives: Read division both ways — equal sharing and grouping — and see each as undoing a multiplication
Execute long division as the multiply–subtract–bring-down loop, knowing why each step is lawful and where place value hides
Prove and use the remainder bound r < b, predict a quotient's digit count, and certify any division with the check a = q·b + r and the mod-9 fingerprint
Prove why division by zero has no answer — and why 0 ÷ 0 fails differently from 7 ÷ 0

lessons.title: Order of Operations and the Language of Expressions
concepts: Brackets: bar, parentheses, braces, square brackets
objectives: Read any string of numbers and operations as one expression with a single value — and distinguish expressions from equations
State the order-of-operations treaty: brackets first (bar, then ( ), { }, [ ]), then "of", then × and ÷ left to right, then + and − left to right
Justify why × outranks + by the compression argument, and say precisely which clauses of the treaty are forced and which are agreed
Simplify fully nested exam expressions with the bracket ladder, dodging the two great BODMAS traps
Gate every simplification with a rounding estimate before trusting it

chapters.title: Factors, Multiples and Primes
chapters.summary: The multiplicative structure of whole numbers: divisibility tests with reasons, prime factorisation, HCF and LCM by three routes, and a first meeting with the infinitude of primes.

lessons.title: Divisibility and Its Tests
concepts: Compound tests and the coprime split
objectives: Define divisibility through the division algorithm of Lesson 2.4 — d divides n exactly when the remainder is 0 — and use the d | n notation
Apply the tail tests for 2, 5, 10, 4, 25, 8 and 125, and derive them from the fact that 10^k = 2^k × 5^k
Prove the digit-sum tests for 9 and 3, apply the alternating-sum test for 11, and read actual remainders off both
Screen any number against every divisor from 2 to 12 in seconds, using the cheapest test first — and know why the parts in a compound test must be coprime

lessons.title: Prime Numbers and Factorisation
concepts: Why 1 and 0 sit outside the treaty
Trial division and the square-root licence
objectives: Define prime and composite numbers by counting factors, and explain why 1 (and 0) belong to neither family
Run the sieve of Eratosthenes up to 100 and recall the 25 primes it leaves behind
Certify primality by trial division, using the square-root licence to stop testing at √n — and spot the false primes 91, 87 and 221
Factorise any number completely into primes and state the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every road reaches the same atoms
Predict the number of divisors of any number from its prime exponents, via (a₁ + 1)(a₂ + 1)⋯(aₖ + 1)

lessons.title: Highest Common Factor
concepts: HCF as the greatest common divisor
Shared primes at the smaller powers
Bézout's identity and the crossroads lemma
objectives: Define common factors and the highest common factor, and read the HCF off two prime factorisations as the shared primes taken at the smaller powers
Run the Euclidean division method — the ladder of remainders — for two and three numbers, and justify it with the swap lemma
State Bézout's identity, prove it by back-substitution, and use it to discharge the crossroads-lemma debt that Lesson 3.2 left open
Generalise Lesson 3.1's coprime split into a theorem and deploy the three "greatest number" patterns that examinations recycle

lessons.title: Lowest Common Multiple
concepts: LCM as the first shared departure
Shared primes at the larger powers
objectives: Define common multiples and the lowest common multiple, and prove that the common multiples of a pair are exactly the multiples of their LCM
Compute the LCM by three routes — listing, prime factorisation at the larger powers, and the common-division ladder — and choose the right route for the job
Read the LCM off the Venn picture Lesson 3.3 drew, as the product of all three territories, and recognise the coprime and divisibility extremes
Deploy the four "least number" exam patterns — exact division, same remainder, equal deficiencies, and counting multiples — with reasons

lessons.title: HCF, LCM and How They Relate
concepts: Feasibility: the HCF must divide the LCM
objectives: Prove the product rule gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b from the Venn territories and the atoms
Rebuild a missing member from HCF, LCM and the known member — with the guard that the HCF divides every member
Rebuild whole pairs with the coprime-split engine, and count how many pairs share one fingerprint
Test any fingerprint for feasibility with one division, and unite the chapter's exam patterns in a single table

chapters.title: Fractions
chapters.summary: Why we need numbers between the integers, what a fraction really is, equivalence, comparison, the four operations on fractions, and the number line made dense.

lessons.title: The Idea of a Fraction
concepts: Fractions name parts of a whole
objectives: Say precisely what a fraction is — both as equal parts of a whole and as an exact division — and name its parts (numerator, denominator, vinculum)
Place any fraction on the number line between the right whole numbers, and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers using the division algorithm of Lesson 2.4
Compute a fraction of a quantity, and read "how many 1/d-pieces fit in m" as the grouping division of Lesson 2.4
Prove that between any two different fractions there always lies another — the density that Lesson 3.5 promised — using the mediant

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions and Simplification
objectives: Recognise and generate equivalent fractions with the multiplying rule n/d = nk/dk, and explain it by regrouping equal pieces
Simplify any fraction to its lowest terms in one step via the HCF of chapter 3, and say why that name is the canonical one
Prove the cross-multiplication test a/b = c/d ⟺ ad = bc — paying, in full, the licence Lesson 4.1 borrowed for the mediant proof
Raise a fraction to any target denominator that is a multiple of its own — the move that powers common denominators in Lessons 4.3–4.4

lessons.title: Comparing Fractions
concepts: Unit fractions shrink as denominators grow
objectives: Decide which of two fractions with the same denominator or the same numerator is larger, and justify the verdict in terms of piece size and count
Compare any two positive fractions with the cross-multiplication test — two multiplications — and say why the products decide, on the common bd-ruler
Raise any set of fractions to one common ruler (the product of denominators or the LCM) and arrange them in ascending or descending order
Use the anchors 0, 1/2 and 1, the completing-the-whole view, and the wholes-first rule to compare mixed numbers and exam-style lists quickly

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
concepts: Unlike fractions and the LCM method
Sums and differences in lowest terms
objectives: Add and subtract fractions on a shared ruler by counting pieces, and simplify every result to lowest terms
Raise any two unlike fractions to one common ruler — the LCM as standard equipment — and add or subtract the raised counts, with mixed numbers handled storey by storey
Read subtraction as gap-naming and complements, and decide when a subtraction has an answer at all
Split fractions into two-term sums of distinct unit fractions by the greedy choice, and prove why adding straight across never works

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
objectives: Multiply fractions straight across and simplify, read 'of' chains left to right, and cancel atoms before multiplying to keep every count small
Predict what multiplication does to size — proper multipliers shrink, improper ones grow, 1 holds — and verify the commutative, associative, identity and zero laws on fractions
Divide by any fraction through the reciprocal theorem, with the bd-ruler measurement count as the proof and the sharing reading as the small-divisor check
Compute the HCF and LCM of fractions with the banked shortcuts, push mixed numbers through the improper conversion, and settle exam word problems of the bottle, tank and ribbon families

chapters.title: Decimals and Percents
chapters.summary: Place value extended to the right of the point, the natural marriage of decimals and fractions, percent as a standardised fraction of 100, and the practical arithmetic of increase, decrease, discount and interest.
plannedLessons: Percentage Change, Discounts and Simple Interest

lessons.title: Decimal Places and the Point
concepts: The decimal point as a landmark
The atom test for exact decimal dress
objectives: Explain what the decimal point marks, read any decimal aloud correctly, and write decimals in expanded form across the extended place-value chart
Convert both ways across the fraction–decimal bridge: 10-family denominators directly, and any denominator built from 2s and 5s by re-cutting with the multiplying rule of Lesson 4.2
Prove and apply the atom test — a lowest-terms fraction wears an exact decimal dress if and only if its denominator carries no atoms but 2s and 5s, and the dress needs max(m, n) places
Locate decimals on the number line by zooming, compare and order them by aligning the points, and convert money, length and mass without the zero-filling traps

lessons.title: Decimals and Fractions, Two Ways of Writing the Same Numbers
concepts: Long division as the decimal machine
objectives: Run the long-division step machine past the point — multiply the remainder by ten, divide, record the digit — and justify why each step is legal
Classify any fraction in advance: terminating in max(m, n) places (only 2s and 5s), pure recurring (no 2s or 5s), or mixed recurring (a head of max(m, n) places, then a cycle)
Prove the dresses theorem by the pigeonhole argument on remainders, and read cycle lengths as the order of 10 modulo the denominator
Convert every recurring decimal back to its fraction by shift-and-subtract, and compare recurring decimals with truncated ones without being fooled

chapters.title: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
chapters.summary: Comparing quantities by division rather than difference: ratios in simplest form, unit rates, the cross-multiplication test for proportion, direct and inverse variation, and scaling in maps, recipes and models.

chapters.title: Integers
chapters.summary: Negative numbers earn their place on the number line: temperatures, debts and directions; the sign rules derived rather than memorised; absolute value as distance; and the coordinate plane preview.
plannedLessons: Negative Numbers and Why They Exist
Multiplying Integers and the Sign Rules

chapters.title: Geometry Foundations
chapters.summary: The visual half of mathematics begins: points, lines, planes and angles as ideal objects; measuring angles; parallel lines and transversals; triangles and the angle-sum result; and the first area formulas, derived.
plannedLessons: Perimeter and Area of Rectangles, Triangles and Circles

chapters.title: Measurement
chapters.summary: What it means to measure: units as agreements, the metric system from first principles, unit conversion as multiplication by one, and the difference between precision and accuracy.
plannedLessons: Precision, Accuracy and Rounding in Measurement

chapters.title: Data and Graphs
chapters.summary: Reading the world in tables and pictures: frequency tables, bar charts, line graphs, pie charts and when each lies or tells the truth; the mean, median and mode introduced honestly with their strengths and traps.
plannedLessons: Bar Charts, Line Graphs and Pie Charts

chapters.title: Patterns and the Doorstep of Algebra
chapters.summary: Number patterns, sequences built by rules, matchstick and tile patterns expressed as formulas, and the first use of a letter for an unknown — the exact point where Elementary Algebra takes over the climb.
